newsitem.title: FRANCE: French deputies adopt key immigration amendment.
newsitem.headline: French deputies adopt key immigration amendment.

text.p: French deputies on Wednesday approved a key amendment softening an immigration bill that has sparked heated debate inside parliament and violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police outside.

Boosted by its strong majority, the centre-right government pushed the amendment through by 163 votes for to 63 against, dropping a requirement that French citizens must report to the town hall the departure of their foreign guests.

Instead, guests will themselves have to report their departure to police. The amendement also shifts from mayors to the prefects (local government representatives) the responsibility for keeping stays by foreigners under control.

Thirty riot police were hurt, including one who lost a finger, and 40 protesters were detained in clashes near the National Assembly building after demonstrators began throwing stones and other projectiles on Tuesday night, police said.

The street violence, which contrasted with a large peaceful demonstration against the immigration bill on Saturday, mirrored the invective inside the chamber which forced Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin to call hecklers repeatedly to order.

To loud boos from government benches, Communist deputy Maxime Gremetz said provisions which allow for raids on workplaces, to crack down on illegal labour, harked back to the collaborationist Vichy regime of the Second World War.
Socialist spokesman Jean Glavany raised the tension a little later by referring to "the dark hours of the Republic".
"If you tell young French people that Vichy is what we are living through, you give them a dangerously positive idea of this historical tragedy," Education Minister Francois Bayrou retorted.
Tuesday night's Paris violence came at the end of a peaceful march to demand the withdrawal of the bill, which police said drew 16,000 protesters while organisers claimed 30,000.
There were no figures for injuries to protesters. Five of the 40 detainees remained in custody on Wednesday.

There was also violence in Toulouse, where police used tear gas to disperse demonstrators protesting against both the bill and the presence in their southern city of the number two of the far-right National Front, Bruno Megret.
Toulouse police said five police officers were injured.

Anger over the bill spread to the diplomatic front when the president of the European Parliament cancelled a meeting with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette after several French officials, including de Charette, attacked the parliament for becoming involved and urging the immigration bill be withdrawn.
De Charette said the European Parliament was "not yet a parliament worthy of the name".
Jose-Maria Gil-Robles, a Spanish conservative, branded de Charette's words "an unacceptable judgment on the European Parliament, its role and its dignity".

French President Jacques Chirac, during a meeting with Gil-Robles on Tuesday, had accused the parliament of "unacceptable interference" in French affairs for adopting the motion critical of the immigration measure.

The bill, opposed by groups from artists to human rights campaigners, aims to close loopholes in tough existing laws dating from 1993 and would grant the police extended powers to track immigrants in France.
The opposition has accused the conservative government of pandering to growing numbers of National Front voters with the approach of a general election in 1998.

Socialists and Communists, largely absent when the Assembly first debated the bill in December, are trying to delay or alter the bill with a flood of amendments. But government supporters hold four-fifths of the 577 seats.
